title: Grace (ST I-II.109–114)
hook: we need God's help both to know and to do the good fully

segments.voice: Yesterday, do good, avoid evil: Thomas's first principle, a light already on in the mind. Your line was the first principle. Where did you ask which way was the good? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

A couch is wedged in a doorway, one arm through, one arm stuck. The person moving it has pushed, lifted, tilted, and sworn at it. It isn't that they're weak. They got it down the hall alone, and up the porch steps. But there's a point where one person, however strong, can't finish the job. Then a neighbor walks by, grabs the other end, says pivot, and the couch slides through. Yesterday Thomas said the light of right and wrong is already on in us. Today he asks the harder question: is the light enough? His answer is grace.
screen: `A COUCH STUCK IN THE DOORWAY.` → `STRONG, BUT NOT ENOUGH.` → `IS THE LIGHT ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: Thomas opens his treatise on grace with a careful question: what can a person do without it? And the answer is not nothing. He says people can know many true things by the natural light of the mind. Even after the fall, he says, people can do some particular goods by their own powers. His examples are wonderfully ordinary: building houses, planting vineyards. Then the turn. Doing some good is not the same as doing the whole good. Thomas compares fallen human nature to a sick person who can move around a little, but can't move freely until medicine heals him. So grace does two jobs. It heals what's wounded, and it lifts us toward a good beyond our nature: friendship with God, the charity of three days ago. No amount of pushing gets the couch through that door alone. Thomas goes further. Even turning toward God in the first place, even getting ready for grace, is itself God's help at work. Paul says it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "For it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will." And Jesus, in John: "without me you can do nothing." One more line, from the very start of the Summa, keeps this from sounding grim: grace does not destroy nature, Thomas says, but perfects it. Grace isn't God shoving us aside to do the job himself. It's the other end of the couch. Look back over these days: justice, fortitude, temperance, charity. Each is something a person grows in. Today Thomas names the help underneath them.
screen: `NOT NOTHING: HOUSES AND VINEYARDS.` · `SOME GOOD IS NOT THE WHOLE GOOD.` · `GRACE HEALS AND LIFTS.` · `GRACE PERFECTS NATURE.` · then, large: `WITHOUT ME YOU CAN DO NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for help before a task. Get still for a moment. Pick the next real task in front of you: a hard email, a meal to cook, a conversation, a shift at work. Notice where your own strength runs out in it, honestly, without shame. If you pray, you can ask God for help with that task, in your own words or with a prayer you already know, before you start. If you don't pray, think of one person you could ask for help with it, and let yourself be willing to ask. The bell holds the time.
Grace. For Thomas, God's free help, which heals human nature and lifts it toward a good beyond its reach, without destroying it. Today's word.
Your line: help is needed. Today, before one task, ask for help first, from God or from a person, instead of after you're stuck. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of grace as God's free gift, received especially through prayer and the sacraments, and the Church teaches that even the first turning toward God is moved by grace.

original.note: Greek, the word Paul uses for grace: favor, a gift freely given.

trapdoor: what you thought: grace means being elegant, or a prayer before dinner.
what it means: God's free help, which heals human nature and lifts it toward a good beyond its reach.
what a scholar hears: Thomas's sick-man image, and his maxim from the Summa's first question: grace perfects nature, not destroys it.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: knowing truth by natural light (I-II.109.1); in the state of corrupt nature, man can do some particular good, 'such as to build dwellings, plant vineyards', but not all the good natural to him, like a sick man who can move somewhat but not perfectly until healed (109.2); grace as healing and elevating (109.2); preparation for grace itself requires God's help (109.6); 'grace does not destroy nature but perfects it' (I.1.8 ad 2).
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Philippians 2:13 and John 15:5 (fragment).
